newsitem.title: BURUNDI: Trial into killing of Burundi president reopens.
newsitem.headline: Trial into killing of Burundi president reopens.

text.p: The Supreme Court restarted a trial on Friday of 79 people charged with killing Burundi's first freely-elected Hutu president but one defendant laughed off the charges.
Supreme Court Chief Justice Salvator Scromba said in the capital Bujumbura that the 79 accused, many of whom were military officers, were charged with mutiny. All have pleaded not guilty.
Ethnic Tutsi troops murdered president Melchior Ndadaye during an attempted coup in Bujumbura in October 1993, sparking a wave of revenge killings by Hutus and army repression.
Since then more than 150,000 people have been killed in massacres and civil war pitting the Tutsi-dominated army against rebels of the Hutu majority.

Tutsi-dominated Uprona party member of parliament Francois Ngeze, named president for two days after Ndadaye's death, said he had no prior knowledge of the coup and would have been killed had he declined the post.

"I was not informed about the coup. That night I was woken by the sound of gunfire. Then the army surrounded my house and took me away," said Ngeze, producing from a briefcase a pair of red pyjamas he said he was wearing at the time.
"Was I going to be president in pyjamas," he asked the packed courtroom to laughter.

Former army chief of staff Colonel Jean Bikomagu, singled out by a 1996 U.N. report into Ndadaye's murder, also hotly denied the charges. Bikomagu handed over Ndadaye to the soldiers who killed him, the U.N. report said.
"I categorically deny these allegations. I did what I could to protect Ndadaye. When I asked soldiers not to kill the president, they threatened to kill me," he said.

Military leader Pierre Buyoya began the trial earlier this year to balance parallel proceedings against leading members of the pro-Hutu Frodebu party over killings after the 1993 coup bid, a foreign expert on Burundi said.
Buyoya, who himself seized power in an army coup a year ago and deposed Burundi's Hutu president Sylvestre Ntibantunganya, called in May for a U.N. tribunal in May into the events of October 1993.
Only about half the defendants appeared in court on Friday. The trial was adjourned, but no date was set for it to reopen.
Buyoya said this week he would soon open direct talks with armed groups, a move opposed by many fellow ethnic Tutsis who hold Hutu political groups responsible for genocide after the coup attempt.
